definition: A reactive dye is a colorant carrying a chemical group that forms a covalent bond with the fiber, most importantly with hydroxyl groups of cellulose in cotton and viscose.
explanation: A reactive dye has a chromophore, water-solubilizing sulfonate groups, and one or more reactive groups such as a halotriazine or vinyl sulfone. In an exhaust process, salt drives dye onto cellulose, and alkali then ionizes cellulose hydroxyls so they attack the reactive group, fixing the dye by covalent bond. The same alkali also lets water compete, hydrolyzing some dye so it can no longer react. That hydrolyzed dye must be washed off thoroughly or it bleeds in later washing.
example: A dyehouse colors cotton jersey bright turquoise. Fixation leaves part of the dye hydrolyzed in the bath and loosely held in the fabric. If rinsing and soaping are cut short to save water, the garment may pass the lab dye check yet stain a white shirt in its first home wash. The dye chemistry was sound; the removal of unfixed dye was not.
caution: Covalent fixation gives good wash fastness but does not guarantee lightfastness or chlorine resistance, which depend on the chromophore. Reactive dyeing uses large amounts of salt and alkali and leaves colored effluent from hydrolyzed dye. Reactive is a dye class, not a sustainability claim, and dyes marketed as low-salt or high-fixation are producer claims to check.
deeper: Two reaction types dominate. Halotriazine dyes react by nucleophilic substitution: the cellulosate anion displaces chloride or fluoride on the triazine ring. Vinyl sulfone dyes, formed from a sulfatoethylsulfone precursor under alkali, react by nucleophilic addition across the double bond. Hydroxide in the bath competes with cellulosate, so fixation efficiency is always below 100 percent. Bifunctional dyes with two reactive groups aim to raise fixation. A review of fiber-dye chemistry notes that cellulose's relative inertness toward dyes necessitates chemical auxiliaries, and that effluent contains unreacted dye and high salt loads. Research dyes with vinyl sulfone centers show fixation varying strongly with pH, temperature and time. Because reactive-dyed cotton fibers look morphologically alike, forensic laboratories identify them by extracting and analyzing the dye.
origins: Reactive dyes are a comparatively recent class. Earlier dyes for cellulose, such as direct and vat dyes, relied on physical affinity or insolubilization in the fiber rather than a chemical bond. Commercial dyes designed to bond covalently with cellulose arrived in the mid twentieth century and became a leading route for bright cotton shades. This edition could not verify the specific inventors and launch dates, so they are omitted.

definition: Reeling unwinds the continuous filaments of several softened silk cocoons at once and combines them into a single raw silk thread of controlled size, wound onto a reel.
explanation: Stifled cocoons are first cooked in hot water or steam to soften the sericin so the filament unwinds without breaking, and loose outer floss is brushed away to find each filament end. The reeler draws the ends of several cocoons together through guides. While still soft, the sericin acts as a glue as the thread passes through a croissure, where it is crossed on itself or with a second thread to press out water and bond the filaments into one compact strand. As cocoons run out, new ends are joined in to keep the thread size constant.
example: A reeler working to a target raw silk size watches the thread as it forms. Filaments get finer toward the inner layers of each cocoon, so she adds a fresh cocoon before the combined size drifts low. That attention decides whether the finished fabric will later show uneven streaks or look uniform.
caution: Reeled silk is different from spun silk, which is carded and spun from short lengths out of broken or pierced cocoons and reeling waste. Raw silk from the reel still carries its sericin and must be degummed. Raw silk denier describes the combined thread, not one cocoon filament. Reeling also differs from throwing, the later twisting and plying of raw silk.
deeper: Individual cocoon filaments average only about 1.5 to 3.5 denier, so thread size is built by combining filaments from roughly 2 to 20 cocoons, depending on the target. In common practice the reeling basin is held at around 40 to 45 C, with cooking done separately. The croissure gives cohesion by rubbing the composite thread rather than by adding lasting twist. The FAO reports total cocoon filament lengths of about 600 to 1,500 m, of which about 80 percent is typically reelable; the remainder becomes waste used for spun silk. Automatic reeling machines monitor thread size and feed new cocoon ends mechanically.
origins: Reeling is as old as silk textiles themselves, beginning as hand reeling from a basin of hot water in China and spreading with sericulture. Equipment progressed from hand-turned reels to foot-powered reels and then to multi-basin filatures in mechanized silk factories, and later to automatic reeling machines. The general English word reel names a winding frame; in silk it specifically denotes this combined unwinding and joining step.

definition: A family of farming and grazing approaches aimed at rebuilding soil health, biodiversity and ecosystem processes, which still lacks a consensus definition or a single standardized certification.
explanation: Regenerative agriculture is usually defined in one of two ways: by practices, such as reduced tillage, cover crops, diverse rotations, organic amendments and integrated livestock or managed grazing, or by outcomes, such as rising soil organic matter, better nutrient and water cycling and greater biodiversity. Fiber claims mostly involve cotton, wool and other animal fibers from farms in such programs. Unlike organic agriculture, which regulated certification defines largely by permitted inputs, regenerative claims mean whatever the program or standard behind them specifies.
example: Two wool suppliers both describe their farms as regenerative. One cites enrollment in a program that monitors soil and vegetation indicators at fixed sites over years; the other cites a set of adopted grazing practices without measurements. A student should ask which program applies, what is verified and by whom, and whether the fiber delivered is traceable to those farms.
caution: Regenerative is not a synonym for organic, carbon neutral or certified; a regenerative claim can exist with or without any of these. Soil carbon gains are slow, variable and reversible, so sequestration claims deserve particular scrutiny. Scholars note that a definition based on a practice list is easier to certify but also easier to use as a marketing label. Without a named standard and verification, the word alone conveys little that can be checked.
deeper: Definitions in the literature fall into practice-based and outcome-based families, and researchers have identified several distinct discourses behind them. A 2025 proposal instead frames regenerative agriculture as an ecological ethic and approach that supports ecosystem processes, arguing that whether a site is regenerating depends on site-specific measurement of its trajectory and rate of change over time. A 2025 review estimated adoption at under 1% of global farmed acreage and named an unresolved operational definition and the lack of standardized certification as barriers. Measuring soil carbon change requires sampling to a stated depth, bulk density data and repeat sampling at the same sites, because changes are small relative to existing stocks and vary across a field.
origins: One 2025 review describes the concept as formalized more than 40 years ago while drawing on much older Indigenous land-care philosophies. Early academic definitions tied it to rising soil biological productivity, low external inputs and organic farming. Calls for regenerative agriculture have increased sharply in recent years, including in food and fiber supply chains, which is why scholars now debate whether it should be defined by practices, by outcomes or by an underlying ethic.
